readerTitle: Nine goals on a café whiteboard, and why one is enough
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 카페, 예약 앱 팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 적용 레슨: 하는 일이 너무 많을 때의 비용(OPS-04-05), 목표와 핵심 결과(OPS-04-02)
insight: 좋은 목표 설정은 무엇을 할지 고르는 일보다 무엇을 이번 분기에 하지 않을지 정하고, 남은 하나를 숫자로 확인할 수 있는 결과로 바꾸는 일이다.
misconception: 목표를 많이 세울수록 더 많이 이룬다. 할 일 목록(행사 시작, 메뉴 출시)이 곧 목표다.

sources.text: Grove, A. (1983). High Output Management. (목표와 핵심 결과의 원형)
Doerr, J. (2018). Measure What Matters. (OKR 개념 정리)
모든 수치와 장면은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 카페 오후 매출: 현재 $180 ÷ 25명 = 객단가 $7.20, 목표 $300 ÷ 40명 = $7.50. 두 핵심 결과가 서로 모순되지 않는지 확인했습니다.
앱 팀 예시: 신규 가입자의 7일 내 첫 예약 비율 30% → 45%는 가상 수치입니다. 실제 업계 평균처럼 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.
OKR의 기원(Intel, Andy Grove)은 OPS-04-09와 겹치지 않도록 이 레슨에서는 언급하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Nine goals on a café whiteboard
body: It's January. Maya owns a small café near an office park. On the back-room whiteboard she writes her goals for the next three months.
New lunch menu. Loyalty card. Catering. Weekend brunch. Instagram. Busier afternoons. Lower waste. Staff training. A second espresso machine.
Every one of them is a good idea. That's the problem.

image.label: A café back-room whiteboard crowded with nine goals
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 카페 뒷방. 화이트보드에 손글씨로 목표 9개가 빽빽하게 적혀 있고, 주인이 마커를 든 채 서 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고나 컵 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Maya do with the list?
body: She has four staff, about ten spare hours a week of her own, and a small budget. How should she set the quarter's goals?

options.text: Keep all nine and give each staff member two to own
options.feedback: This is **the cost of doing too much** at work. Everything starts, attention gets split nine ways, and by March most goals are half-done.

options.text: Pick one goal for the quarter and park the other eight
options.feedback: Focus has a price: eight good ideas wait. In return, the one that matters most gets real time and money, and you can tell if it worked.

options.text: Pick the top three and treat them as equal
options.feedback: Far better than nine. But with ten spare hours a week, three equal goals still means about three hours each. Ranking them would help.

cards.title: Find the goal that unlocks the most.
body: Maya looks at her sales by hour. Mornings are packed. Lunch is fine. From 2 to 5 p.m. on weekdays, the café is nearly empty, yet rent and staff cost the same.
She picks that. Several parked ideas, like a loyalty card or an afternoon menu, might even become ways to fix it later.
Her objective for the quarter: **Make weekday afternoons worth opening for.**

cards.title: An objective needs results you can count.
body: An **objective** says where you want to go, in plain words. **Key results** are two or three numbers that show whether you got there.
The test for a key result: at the end of the quarter, could anyone look at it and say yes or no without arguing?
"Make afternoons better" fails that test. A number with a start point and a target passes it.

image.label: One objective at the top, two measurable key results below
image.brief: 간단한 도식. 위쪽 큰 상자에 "Objective: Make weekday afternoons worth opening for", 아래에 숫자가 들어간 작은 상자 2개가 화살표로 연결됨. 카페 컵 아이콘을 작게 곁들임.

cards.title: Which is a real key result?
body: Today, weekday afternoons bring in about $180 from about 25 customers. Which line belongs under Maya's objective?

options.feedback: A useful idea, but it's a task, not a result. You could launch it perfectly and still have an empty café. In **objectives and key results**, tasks serve the numbers.

options.text: Raise average weekday 2–5 p.m. sales from $180 to $300
options.feedback: It has a start, a target and a clear yes or no. This is how a **key result** should read. The cost: you might miss it, and everyone will see.
Easy to agree with, impossible to check. In March, Maya and her staff could each argue it either way.

cards.title: One objective, two key results, many experiments.
list: **Objective:** Make weekday afternoons worth opening for
**Key result 1:** Weekday 2–5 p.m. sales from $180 to $300
**Key result 2:** Afternoon customers from 25 to 40 a day
cards.callout: The pastry deal, a quiet study corner and a flyer for nearby offices are now experiments. Keep the ones that move the numbers.

cards.title: Focus can hide what you stopped watching.
body: While everyone chases afternoons, the morning rush still pays the bills. Maya keeps an eye on a few everyday numbers, like morning wait times and food waste, so they don't quietly slip.
She also sets a check-in at week six. If afternoons haven't moved at all, that's information too. Maybe the answer is shorter afternoon hours, not more customers.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app.
body: A three-person team runs an app for booking fitness classes. Many new users sign up but never book. Which goal setup is strongest for the quarter?

options.text: Objective: Grow. Key results: ship six features, redesign onboarding, start a blog
options.feedback: Three people, many tasks, no outcome. This combines **too much** with key results that are really a to-do list.

options.text: Objective: New users get value in their first week. Key result: share who book within 7 days, from 30% to 45%
options.feedback: One focus and a countable result. Features and onboarding changes become experiments judged by that number.

options.text: Five objectives covering growth, retention, revenue, hiring and brand
options.feedback: Each is worthy, and the team can see the whole picture. But five objectives for three people spreads attention just like Maya's nine.

cards.title: Pick one, then make it countable.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **The cost of doing too much** told Maya to park eight goals. **Objectives and key results** turned the one left into numbers she can check.
**Try it today:** write your goals for the next three months. Circle one. Under it, write two numbers with a start point and a target.
